title: 1 Samuel 15:10–23
context: The LORD tells Samuel that he grieves over having made Saul king, because Saul has turned back from following him. Samuel, angry and grieved, cries out all night, then goes to meet Saul, who has set up a monument for himself at Carmel and gone down to Gilgal. Saul claims he has obeyed, blames the people for the spared livestock, and says it was kept for sacrifice. Samuel answers that obeying the LORD’s voice is better than sacrifice, and that because Saul rejected the LORD’s word, the LORD has rejected him as king.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came to Samuel, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to Samuel. Arminian readers note that God speaks to his prophet in response to what Saul has done, showing that the LORD is actively engaged with events as they unfold in Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the word of the LORD as the decisive factor in the story, interpreting Saul’s actions before Saul gives his own account. Both traditions read the verse as introducing the divine verdict that frames the confrontation that follows.

verses.text: “It grieves me that I have set up Saul to be king, for he has turned back from following me, and has not performed my commandments.” Samuel was angry; and he cried to the LORD all night.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says it grieves him that he made Saul king, because Saul turned back. Arminian readers see real divine sorrow over a king’s free disobedience. The same Hebrew verb returns in 15:29 and 15:35; see the note at 15:29.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm God’s real displeasure while reading the grief language alongside 15:29, where he does not change his mind. Shared ground: God takes Saul’s disobedience seriously, and Samuel’s all-night cry shows the weight of the moment.

verses.text: Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning; and Samuel was told, saying, “Saul came to Carmel, and behold, he set up a monument for himself, turned, passed on, and went down to Gilgal.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul goes to Carmel, sets up a monument for himself, and goes on to Gilgal. Arminian readers note that this Carmel is a town in the hill country of Judah (compare 25:2), not Mount Carmel in the north.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the monument as revealing Saul’s concern for his own glory after a victory God had given. Both traditions read the detail as a quiet indictment, placed just before Saul claims to have obeyed the LORD completely.

verses.text: Samuel came to Saul; and Saul said to him, “You are blessed by the LORD! I have performed the commandment of the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul greets Samuel with a blessing and claims to have performed the LORD’s command. Arminian readers see self-deception or evasion, as Saul either does not see or does not admit what he has left undone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see how readily sin justifies itself with religious language. Shared ground: Saul’s claim of full obedience is false, and the narrative lets readers see the gap between his words and his actions before Samuel names it.

verses.text: Samuel said, “Then what does this bleating of the sheep in my ears and the lowing of the cattle which I hear mean?”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel asks about the bleating sheep and lowing cattle. Arminian readers note the vivid irony: the evidence of Saul’s disobedience is audible, undermining his claim the moment he makes it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet’s question as exposing hidden sin, a pattern in which God brings to light what people try to cover. Both traditions read the question as a simple, devastating challenge to Saul’s account of what he did.

verses.text: Saul said, “They have brought them from the Amalekites; for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the cattle, to sacrifice to the LORD your God. We have utterly destroyed the rest.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul blames the people and says they spared the best to sacrifice to the LORD. Arminian readers note that he shifts responsibility and speaks of “the LORD your God,” distancing himself from the God he claims to serve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an attempt to cover disobedience with worship, treating sacrifice as a substitute for obedience. Shared ground: Saul’s excuse uses religious language to defend a choice God had forbidden, which Samuel will soon answer.

verses.text: Then Samuel said to Saul, “Stay, and I will tell you what the LORD said to me last night.” He said to him, “Say on.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel tells Saul to stop and hear what the LORD said in the night. Arminian readers note that Samuel interrupts Saul’s excuses, refusing to let the conversation continue on Saul’s terms before God’s word is spoken.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophetic word cutting through human self-justification. Both traditions read Saul’s response, “Say on,” as a reluctant opening for the verdict, with Samuel now speaking with the authority of what God revealed.

verses.text: Samuel said, “Though you were little in your own sight, weren’t you made the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel;
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel reminds Saul that he was small in his own eyes when the LORD made him head of the tribes. Arminian readers see a contrast between Saul’s earlier humility (9:21) and his present self-exaltation at Carmel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul’s position came entirely from the LORD’s anointing, not from his own greatness. Shared ground: the reminder exposes how far Saul has moved from the humble beginning of his reign under God’s appointment.

verses.text: and the LORD sent you on a journey, and said, ‘Go, and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they are consumed.’
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel restates the command to destroy the sinners, the Amalekites, until they were consumed. Arminian readers note that the mission was clear and specific, leaving no room for Saul’s claim of misunderstanding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Amalek is called “sinners,” framing the command as judgment rather than as conquest for gain. Both traditions read the verse as restating a unique command tied to Amalek’s history, not a general principle.

verses.text: Why then didn’t you obey the LORD’s voice, but took the plunder, and did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight?”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel asks why Saul did not obey but took the plunder and did evil. Arminian readers note that the charge links disobedience with greed, since rushing on the plunder shows what Saul and the people actually valued.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase “evil in the LORD’s sight” placing Saul under the same judgment as Israel in Judges. Shared ground: Samuel names the sin directly, and both traditions read the question as the core indictment of Saul’s conduct.

verses.text: Saul said to Samuel, “But I have obeyed the LORD’s voice, and have gone the way which the LORD sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul insists he obeyed, went where he was sent, brought Agag, and destroyed Amalek. Arminian readers note that he repeats his defense instead of admitting fault, even mentioning Agag as if sparing him were obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the persistence of self-justification even when confronted with the truth. Both traditions read Saul’s defense as a partial obedience presented as full obedience, which the next verses will expose and reject.

verses.text: But the people took of the plunder, sheep and cattle, the best of the devoted things, to sacrifice to the LORD your God in Gilgal.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul again blames the people for taking the best of the devoted things to sacrifice at Gilgal. Arminian readers note the phrase “devoted things,” which shows that Saul knew these were set apart for destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the attempt to use what belonged to God for worship on Saul’s own terms. Shared ground: Saul’s appeal to sacrifice will be answered in the next verse, where Samuel sets obedience above any religious offering.

verses.text: Samuel said, “Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the LORD’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel says that to obey is better than sacrifice and to listen better than the fat of rams. Arminian readers see God desiring a responsive heart, a theme echoed in Psalm 51:16–17, Hosea 6:6, and Micah 6:6–8.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same truth: outward worship without obedience is empty before God. Shared ground: both traditions treat this verse as central and fully agreed, teaching that God values a heart that hears and obeys his word above ritual.

verses.text: For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as idolatry and teraphim. Because you have rejected the LORD’s word, he has also rejected you from being king.”
verses.arminianNotes: Rebellion is likened to witchcraft and stubbornness to idolatry and teraphim, which WEB explains as household idols. Arminian readers see disobedience treated as a form of false worship, placing self-will in God’s place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that because Saul rejected the LORD’s word, the LORD rejected him as king, a judgment that builds on 13:13–14. Both traditions agree that Saul is rejected from the kingship here; the verse concerns his office.
